targets.title: Hindsight is not equal to foresight: The effect of outcome knowledge on judgment under uncertainty.
targets.evidence_quote: We conducted an open data and open material pre-registered replication of Experiment 2 from Fischhoff (1975) with extensions investigating the associations between the hindsight bias with sociodemographic variables and depressive symptoms, and the moderation role of depressive symptoms on hindsight bias.
targets.outcome_quote: We conclude that our study failed to replicate the results of Experiment 2 from Fischhoff (1975). However, a secondary analysis revealed the presence of a hindsight bias phenomenon with a small effect size.

targets.title: Hindsight bias from 3 to 95 years of age.
targets.evidence_quote: For the extensions, we predict that age will positively correlate with hindsight bias, whereas other socio-demographic variables (such as socioeconomic status, gender, occupation, and education) will not (Hypothesis 2). This investigation will provide further evidence for the claim that populations of older ages are more susceptible to hindsight bias (Bernstein et al., 2011; Groß & Bayen, 2021; Pohl et al., 2018), whereas evidence for gender, occupation, and education is not consolidated yet.
targets.outcome_quote: We expected to find a positive correlation between age and hindsight bias, and no correlation with other socio-demographic variables. Contrary to our expectations, no correlation was found between hindsight bias and sociodemographic or depressive symptoms. These results contrast with previous findings showing a higher magnitude of hindsight bias for older adults (Groß, 2013) and a positive correlation between depressive symptoms and hindsight bias (Groß et al., 2017; Groß & Bayen, 2017).

targets.title: Older and younger adults’ hindsight bias after positive and negative outcomes.
targets.evidence_quote: For the extensions, we predict that age will positively correlate with hindsight bias, whereas other socio-demographic variables (such as socioeconomic status, gender, occupation, and education) will not (Hypothesis 2). This investigation will provide further evidence for the claim that populations of older ages are more susceptible to hindsight bias (Bernstein et al., 2011; Groß & Bayen, 2021; Pohl et al., 2018), whereas evidence for gender, occupation, and education is not consolidated yet. Also, we predict that depressive symptoms will be positively correlated with hindsight bias (Hypothesis 3), thus suggesting an interaction between the cognitive mechanisms in depression and the magnitude of the hindsight bias. Finally, considering the previous evidence of higher levels of hindsight bias associated with higher levels of depressive symptoms (Groß et al., 2017; Groß & Bayen, 2021; Haslam & Jayasinghe, 1995), we expect that depressive symptoms will act as a moderator variable of the hindsight bias effect (Hypothesis 4).
